Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

free adjective

at liberty, not a slave or a prisoner

also at liberty, free to, free from

classical

Phaedr. 3.7.27: rēgnāre nōlō, līber ut nōn sim mihi
Cic. Att. 15.16a.1: ab arbitrīs lībera

līber, lībera, līberum

adjective; “free from” with ab or the ablative

Free as against a slave or a prisoner, and free from something: ab arbitrīs lībera, free from onlookers. Free time is tempus līberum (Traupman 52) or ōtium. To be free to do something is licet (licet mihi, I may). Not “costing nothing”: that is grātīs (see free, costing nothing).

Examples

  • age, sī quō abīre est animus, est licentia? — nōn plānē est, inquit. — fruere quae laudās, canis: rēgnāre nōlō, līber ut nōn sim mihi

    ‘Well, if you want to go somewhere, are you allowed?’ ‘Not really,’ he said. ‘Enjoy what you praise, dog: I don’t want to be a king if I can’t be free.’Phaedr. 3.7.25–27

  • quoūsque calceī nusquam, toga fēriāta, līber tōtus diēs?

    how long will it be no shoes, your toga on holiday, the whole day free?Plin. Ep. 7.3.2

See also free, free, available.

SourcesLewis & Short: liber
